text: Use when planning or writing the words of a landing page for one named account (a 1:1 page), before building any section.
note: The only argument/copy skill the site agent has; delivered on every page kind, including campaign pages.

text: A 1:1 page is written for one company and one reader. It works when that reader sees, within a few seconds, that you understand what they are working on, what you offer, and the one thing to do next. Clear beats clever. Short beats complete.
Before you build or write any visible words, read the account's overview and insights pages, the seller's files, and the cloned sections you might use. Then write this block at the top of plan.md:
**Reader:** the one person the page is for, as a role, never a name. One line on a second reader if there is one.
**Insight:** what the account is working on, in its own words, with its source. One insight.
**Priorities:** two or three things the reader cares about, each tied to the research.
**Offer and action:** the one next step, its button label, and its checked link.
**Proof:** the case studies or studies you will use, with links, and why each one matches this account.
**Sections:** up to five. For each: the one question it answers, the cloned section it starts from, and a word budget.
**Left out:** what you chose not to say, and why.
Read this block again before you write each section and again in your final check. If you change your mind, change the plan first and write down why.
An insight is something the account has said or done that your offer speaks to: a budget line, a plan, a project, a hire, a stated goal. Its size or location is not an insight.
The brief may suggest a proof or a structure. Treat it as a suggestion: run the same checks on it, and search the seller's site for a better fit.
note: duplicate of A1 "The brief sets the goal…"

text: Remove sections that do not help this reader decide (brand videos, newsletters, resource lists, general testimonials) instead of filling them.
note: "brand videos" is listed as a section to remove; legacy offers "Video-led" as an argument pattern (see L1b).

text: When no clone can carry the point, use a brand section; leave the point out if neither fits. Record why in the plan.
The usual shape is five sections, as short as the decision allows (rarely more than 600 words):
note: The 10-26 Pallet production page came out at 5 sections, ~440 words.

text: **Hero:** what this is, for this account. Say what it is or what it achieves, who it is for, and one qualifier. A result in the headline needs attributed proof of that result further down the page. One button.
**Their priorities:** two to four short cards. Each starts from their situation in their words, then says what changes.
**How it works:** in their setting, naming their systems where you know them.
**Proof:** attributed to the customer or study it came from, next to the claim it supports.
**Offer:** what they get and the one button.
Every button says what happens ("Request the analysis") and goes to the same checked link.
Never imply the account is already a customer or partner. Never name or describe individual people at the account.
Each section answers its one question from the plan and stays within its word budget.
Audience dilution: the page speaks to everyone instead of this reader.
note: On a segment or event page the reader is a group by design.

text: CTA competition: there is more than one offer or destination.
Feature dumping: capabilities are listed without tying them to this reader's decision.
Buried proposition: the offer appears only below abstract sections.
Swap test: if a sentence would fit any other account unchanged, make it specific or cut it (product facts are the exception).
note: On a 1:many or event page most sentences fit any account by design.

text: Keep as much of its original wording as still fits this account. … Write each rewrite like the same author: same cadence, same register, and roughly the original's length and line count. A slot that held six words wants about six words back.
note: Legacy L5: "A shortage of slots is not a reason to remove the substance or shrink the type."

text: Clear beats clever.
note: R3.4: stays, moves to the copy skill.

text: Prefer the account's own documents (budget, plans, filings, its website) over press about it.
Use their words. Use at most one or two of their own figures on the whole page.
Say what they did in plain words. Never put file names, line codes or claim ids on the page.
The research's notes on how to approach the account (who to call, what to offer, where you overlap or compete) are for you. Never put them on the page.
If a figure needs a condition to be true (it is combined with other costs, it is a reporter's estimate), leave it out rather than explain it.

loc: 3. Find proof on the seller's own site
text: Start with the seller's files. Then search the seller's own website for case studies, customer stories and studies the seller has published: `web_search` with `include_domains` set to the seller's domain.
Prefer, in this order: the same customer; a customer in the same industry and of similar size; a customer in the same situation (same plan type, same system); a study across many customers.
Open the page with `fetch_page`. Take numbers and quotes only from that page, with the customer's name.
Check that the proof fits the claim it sits beside. Read what the customer changed. If the page says "no plan change" and that customer changed its plan, the proof does not fit.
Use only pages the seller published. If nothing fits, use less proof, not weaker proof.
Say whose result it is in the kicker or the source line; keep the heading about the result.
Use the reader's words for their world. Explain a product name the first time you use it.

Keep claims at the strength the evidence allows, from strongest to weakest support: a product fact; what the product can do; a named customer's result; what it could mean for this account ("could"); a forecast for this account (never).
Use "will" only for what certainly happens ("clicking opens the form"). Use "can" for what the product does and "could" for what it might mean for them.
Say what stays and what improves. Do not tell them their current setup is broken.
Notes, caveats, strategy and reasons go in plan.md and your final report, never on the page.
Mystery-box headline: the headline sounds ambitious but does not say what the offer is.
Investor pitch: the copy talks about the category instead of value to this reader.
Benefit inflation: a capability is written as a guaranteed result.
Metric mutation: a source number has been turned into a different claim.
Unattributed proof: a number appears without whose result it was.
False relationship: wording suggests the account is already a customer or partner.
Negative assumption: the page says their current setup is failing without evidence.
Jargon stacking: several product or industry terms appear without plain explanation.
Redundant subheadline: the supporting line repeats the headline.
Generic CTA: a button says "Learn more" instead of what happens.
Form creep: the form asks for more than the next step needs.
Start every section from the closest cloned section of the seller's site. Keep its layout, images and rhythm.
